NOW, on this 12th day of December 2008, this matter comes before the Administrator of the
Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division on the Order to Review the Proposed Decision.
I. STATEMENT OF REVIEW.
The record in this docket discloses that on February 1, 2008, the Iowa Department of Public
Safety (DPS) filed an administrative hearing complaint against Bowman Ventures, Inc. (Licensee). The
complaint alleged that on February 2, 2007, the Licensee or an agent or employee of the Licensee sold
or supplied an alcoholic beverage to a person under the legal age, in violation of Iowa Code §
123.49(2)(h). The complaint further alleged that the February 2, 2008, violation was the Licensee’s
second violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) within a period of two years.1
A Notice of Hearing scheduled the matter for a hearing on March 7, 2008. The Licensee
requested and was granted continuance of the matter to April 1, 2008. On that date, a hearing was
1 On October 27, 2006, the Licensee’s employee, Cole Eugene Bultman, was criminally charged and convicted of a
sale-to-minor violation under Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). On February 1, 2007, the Division imposed a $500.00 civil
penalty against the Licensee’s license for a first violation of the section.

held before an administrative law judge (ALJ) in accordance with Iowa Code Chapters 17A and 123.
Assistant Attorney General John Lundquist represented the DPS. The Licensee was represented by
Tammy Bowman (Bowman). Bowman is the sole owner of the Licensee.
On April 22, 2008, the ALJ issued a Proposed Decision which imposed a $1,500 civil penalty against
the Licensee’s license and suspended the license for a period of 30 days. The Licensee’s timely request
for review of the Proposed Decision followed.
On May 27, 2008, the Administrator issued an Order granting the Licensee’s request for
review. The parties were given the opportunity to file exceptions and present briefs in support of their
respective positions. The exceptions and brief of the appealing party were due no later than the close
of business on June 20, 2008. Responsive briefs were due no later than the close of business on July
21, 2008. No exceptions or briefs were filed in the matter.
Upon the motion of a party to the hearing or upon the Administrator’s own motion, the
Administrator may reverse or modify any finding of fact if a preponderance of the evidence will
support a determination to reverse or modify the finding. Iowa Code § 17A.15(3). Moreover, the
Administrator may reverse or modify any conclusion of law that the Administrator finds to be in error.
Id.
II. STATEMENT OF LAW.
The alcoholic beverages industry is highly regulated. Iowa Code Chapter 123 was enacted by
the Iowa Legislature “to protect the welfare, health, peace, morals and safety” of Iowans. Iowa Code §
123.1. All provisions of Chapter 123 are to be “liberally construed for the accomplishment of that
purpose.” Id. The trafficking of alcoholic beverages affects the public’s interest to the extent that it is
2

prohibited except as provided in Chapter 123. Id. It is unlawful to manufacture for sale, possess or
transport liquor, wine or beer except under the terms enumerated in Chapter 123. Iowa Code § 123.2.
“Legal age” is a defined term meaning “twenty-one years of age or more.” Iowa Code
§ 123.3(19). Selling or providing an alcoholic beverage to an underage person without exercising
“reasonable care to ascertain” whether the person is of the legal drinking age, is a violation of
Chapter 123. Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). A violation of Chapter 123 or the rules of the Division by an
employee or agent of the licensee is deemed an act of the licensee and subjects the licensee’s license to a
civil penalty, suspension or revocation. 185 IAC 4.8.
The administrative penalties for violations of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) are set by statute.
Under the statute, the first violation of the section “shall” subject a licensee’s license to a civil penalty in
the amount of $500.2 Iowa Code § 123.50(3)(a). A second violation within two years “shall” subject
the licensee’s license to a $1,500 civil penalty and a 30-day license suspension. Iowa Code §
123.50(3)(b). The statutory penalties become progressively more severe as the number of
sale-to-minor violations increase. A criminal conviction is not a prerequisite to the imposition of a civil
penalty or the suspension or revocation of a license. Iowa Code
§ 123.39(1)(c).
When a licensee establishes that reasonable inquiry was made to determine whether the
purchaser was of legal age, the licensee’s violation for selling the alcoholic beverage to the underage
person is legally excused. Iowa Code § 123.49(3).
III. STATEMENT OF THE ISSUES.
2 When used in a statute, the word “shall” imposes a duty. Iowa Code § 4.1(30)(a).
3

Did the Licensee’s employee violate Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) by selling an alcoholic beverage
to an underage person knowing or failing to exercise reasonable care to ascertain whether the person
was under the legal age?
May the Licensee avoid the $1,500 civil penalty and 30-day license suspension by asserting the
affirmative defense offered through a pilot project of the Division when the TIPS training completed
by the Licensee’s employees was sponsored by a former employee and not by the Division?
IV. STATEMENT OF THE FACTS.
In 2003, the Division obtained a grant from the Governor’s Traffic Safety Bureau to sponsor
“value-added” TIPS training for all on-premises licensees located in Iowa City. TIPS is a national
for-profit program designed to teach servers and sellers of alcoholic beverages how to prevent underage
sales, sales to intoxicated persons and drunk driving. The “value-added” portion of the program was
training about the ordinances and regulations unique to Iowa City and information about the
procedures used in alcohol compliance checks by Iowa City officers. The training was co-taught by
Division employees and Iowa City police officers, all of whom were certified TIPS trainers. Proposed
Decision, pages 2 and 3.
The “value-added” TIPS program was offered in Iowa City in 2003 and 2005, as a pilot project.
As part of the pilot project, the Division offered a limited affirmative defense to licensees if an employee
successfully completed the Division sponsored program, but subsequently sold an alcoholic beverage
to an underage person. Proposed Decision, page 3.
4

Information about the “value-added” TIPS training and affirmative defense was disseminated
to licensees through brochures. The 2003 brochure contained the following information about the
affirmative defense:
TIPS training offered by the Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division through the
pilot project may be used by a licensee for a limited period as an affirmative
defense against civil penalties for alcohol sales to minors. In order for a licensee
to use the defense, the employee cited must have been certified through the
program prior to the offense. The affirmative defense may be used once for
violations occurring after the training takes place and may not be applied to
pending violations. Employees cited for
alcohol sales to minors may not use training as an affirmative defense and will
be subject to the same criminal penalties as those not certified.
The 2005 brochure contained essentially the same information, but specified that use of the affirmative
defense was limited to the two-year period following completion of the program. Licensee’s Exhibits 7
and 8.
During the time that the Division was offering the “valued-added” TIPS program, other
groups were also offering TIPS training in Iowa City. The groups included licensees offering in-house
training and beer wholesalers. Although the training offered by the groups was part of the national
TIPS program, some of the programs were shorter and less thorough than the Division sponsored
program. Moreover, the training did not include the “valued-added” portion offered by the Iowa City
5

Police Department. Only the “value-added” TIPS training with information about Iowa City laws
qualified for the affirmative defense. Proposed Decision, page 4.
On May 23, 2005, Jodie Neuzil (Neuzil) successfully completed an in-house TIPS training
program which was offered by the Iowa City Moose Lodge where Neuzil was employed. After
completing the training, Neuzil received a TIPS certification card indicating Christine Garling as the
TIPS trainer. Garling was neither an employee of the Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division, nor the Iowa
City Police Department.
Sometime later, Neuzil was hired to work as a server in the Licensee’s establishment. During
the interview process, Bowman asked Neuzil if she had been TIPS trained. Neuzil responded that she
had successfully completed a TIPS training program that had been offered by her former employer.
Neuzil offered her TIPS training certification card to Bowman as proof of the training. Licensee’s
Exhibit “A.”
In August 2005, Bowman participated in the “value-added” TIPS training program sponsored
by the Division in conjunction with the Iowa City Police Department. After
successfully completing the training, Bowman received a TIPS training certification card similar to the
card issued to Neuzil. During the training, Bowman was told that the “value-added” training would
act like a “get-out-of-jail-free” card if an owner, employee or agent of the Licensee sold or served an
alcoholic beverage to an underage person. Bowman assumed that Neuzil’s TIPS training was the same
as hers and that the affirmative defense would apply if Neuzil sold or served an alcoholic beverage to an
underage person. Proposed Decision, pages 4 and 5.
6

On February 1, 2007 and February 2, 2007, Iowa City police officers conducted compliance
checks to determine whether establishments would sell or provide an alcoholic beverage to an underage
person. Prior to the compliance checks, the participating underage informants were required to empty
their pockets in the presence of an officer to ensure that they carried only their own valid Iowa driver’s
license and the money provided to them by officers to purchase the alcoholic beverages. Moreover, the
underage informants were instructed to answer truthfully if asked their age and to provide their own
valid Iowa driver’s license if asked for identification. Further, each informant was photographed as
evidence of their appearance on the night of the compliance checks. Proposed Decision, page 5.
On February 2, 2007, several undercover officers and an underage informant entered the
Licensee’s establishment to conduct a compliance check. The informant approached the bar and
ordered a Bud Light from bartender Neuzil. Neuzil got the beer and then asked the informant for
identification. The underage informant produced her own valid driver’s license which was vertically
oriented indicating that the informant was underage on the date of issuance. Moreover, a red band
with the words “under age 21 until 4-15-07,” appeared above the informant’s picture.
Neuzil looked at the license and then sold the beer to the underage informant. A criminal
citation for selling alcohol to an underage person in violation of Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h) was issued
to Neuzil that evening. Following a trial, Neuzil was found not guilty and the charge
against her was dismissed. Proposed Decision, pages 5 and 6. The hearing complaint filed by
the DPS followed on February 1, 2008.
V. ANALYSIS.
7

In the instant case, the ALJ found that the preponderance of the evidence established that
Neuzil, an employee of the Licensee, sold an alcoholic beverage to an underage informant on February
2, 2007. Further, the ALJ found that Neuzil either knew or failed to exercise reasonable care to
ascertain whether the underage informant was of the legal drinking age. Id.
The sale on February 2, 2007, occurred under controlled circumstances with officers and
witnesses present. The driver’s license of the underage informant on the night of the compliance check
was vertically oriented and the words “under 21 until 4.15.07,” appeared in a red banner above the
informant’s picture. In the Proposed Decision, the ALJ found that, based on the photograph taken of
the informant on the night of the compliance check and the informant’s appearance and demeanor at
the hearing, the appearance of the informant was consistent with her age.
The narrower issue in the case, therefore, is whether the in-house TIPS training completed by
Neuzil while working for the Moose Lodge qualifies for the affirmative defense granted under the
“value-added” TIPS training sponsored by the Division. Essentially, the Licensee argues that, because
Neuzil had a current TIPS training card at the time she made the sale to the underage informant, the
Licensee is entitled to assert the affirmative defense for the violation on February 2, 2007.
The Division’s offer, however, has always limited the affirmative defense to the Division sponsored
training that was held in conjunction with the Iowa City Police Department. The affirmative defense
was never intended to extend to any training than the Division’s “value-
added” TIPS training initiative. In that sense, the pilot project was very limited in its scope and
application, and the Division never intended to extend the incentive to all TIPS training.
8

Although Bowman concedes that Neuzil’s TIPS training was offered by her former employer,
Bowman essentially argues that the Licensee was misled by the Divison’s offer of a limited affirmative
defense for sale-to-minor violations under Iowa Code § 123.49(2)(h). The Administrator finds
Bowman’s argument to be without merit. The denial of the affirmative defense in the instant case is
consistent with the statements contained in the Divison’s brochures.
The underage informant had an appearance consistent with her age on the date of the
compliance check. When Neuzil asked the informant for identification, the informant produced her
own valid driver’s license. The license was vertically oriented and reflected the words, “under 21 until
4.15.07.” While Neuzil went through the motions of checking the identification, she either
miscalculated or failed to properly verify the informant’s age. Under no circumstances did Neuzil
exercise reasonable care to ascertain whether the informant was of legal drinking age.
The Administrator sees no legal reason to recognize an affirmative defense in the case.
Moreover, the Administrator believes that the Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law and the
Decision and Order in the case should be affirmed.
VI. ORDER.
For the above-stated reasons, the Administrator of the Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division
FINDS that the Proposed Decision of April 22, 2008, should be AFFIRMED.
IT IS THEREFORE ORDERED that the Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law and the
Decision and Order proposed by the administrative law judge are AFFIRMED and incorporated
herein in their entirety.
9

IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that the civil penalty of $1,500 is due and payable to the
“Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division,” 1918 SE Hulsizer Road, Ankeny, Iowa 50021, on or before
Wednesday, January 22, 2009. Failure to pay the civil penalty by that date shall result in further
administrative proceedings against liquor license number LC0033505.
IT IS FURTHER ORDERED that liquor license number LC0033505 is suspended for a
period of 30 days commencing at 6 AM on Thursday, January 22, 2009, and ending at
6 AM on Saturday, February 21, 2009. The Licensee is hereby notified that liquor, wine and beer shall
not be consumed in or on the licensed premises located at 310 E Prentiss in Iowa City, Iowa during the
suspension. The premises may be used for other lawful purposes during the suspension.
The parties are hereby notified that this Order constitutes final agency action for the purpose
of Iowa Code Chapters 17A and 123. This Order becomes final, unless a party to the hearing files a
Petition for Judicial Review with the Iowa District Court within 30 days from the date of this Order.
Iowa Code § 17A.19.
DATED this 12th day of December 2008, Ankeny, Iowa.

On February 1, 2008, the Iowa Department of Public Safety
(Department) filed a Hearing Complaint against Bowman
Ventures, Inc. d/b/a Fitzpatrick’s (licensee), alleging
that on or about February 2, 2007, the licensee or an
employee or agent of the licensee sold or supplied an
alcoholic beverage, wine or beer to a person under the
legal age, in violation of Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h).
The Hearing Complaint further alleged that this was the
licensee’s second violation of Iowa Code section
123.49(2)(h) within a period of two years.
The hearing was held before the undersigned administrative
law judge on April 1, 2008 at 9:00 a.m. at the office of
the Iowa Department of Commerce, Alcoholic Beverages
Division, 1918 S.E. Hulsizer, Ankeny, Iowa. Assistant
Attorney General John Lundquist represented the Department
of Public Safety (DPS). Bowman Ventures, Inc. was self-
represented by its owner, Tammy Bowman.
THE RECORD
The record includes the Hearing Complaint; Notice of
Hearing; Continuance Order; the testimony of the witnesses,
and the following exhibits:
State Exhibit 1: Iowa City Police Department
Incident Report, 2/2/07
State Exhibit 2: Voluntary Statements, 2/2/07
State Exhibit 3: Citation and Disposition, State of
Iowa v. Jodie Lynn Neuzil

ISSUES
Did the licensee’s employee violate Iowa Code section
123.49(2)(h) by selling an alcoholic beverage to an
underage person knowing or failing to exercise reasonable
care to ascertain whether the person was under the legal
age?
May the licensee avoid the $1500 civil penalty and 30 day
license suspension for a second violation of Iowa Code
section 123.49(2)(h) by asserting the affirmative defense
offered through a pilot project of the Alcoholic Beverages
Division, when the TIPS training completed by its employee
was sponsored by a former employer and not by the Iowa
Alcoholic Beverages Division?
FINDINGS OF FACT
1. Bowman Ventures, Inc. d/b/a Fitzpatrick’s (licensee),
holds Liquor License No. LC-33505 for the premises located
at 310 E. Prentiss in Iowa City, Iowa. Tammy Bowman is the
100% owner of Bowman Ventures, Inc. (Testimony of Tammy
Bowman; State Exhibit 5)
2. Training for Intervention Procedures (TIPS) is a
national for-profit training program owned by Health
Communications, Inc., a Virginia corporation. The TIPS
training program is designed to teach servers and sellers
of alcohol how to prevent underage sales, sales to
intoxicated patrons, and drunk driving. TIPS Training
programs are taught throughout the country by certified
trainers. In order to be certified as a TIPS trainer, a
person must attend a two day workshop given by either a

DIA No. 08DOCBL003
Page 3
TIPS master trainer or by a person from the TIPS central
office. Following the workshop, the person must pass a
certification examination. To maintain certification as a
TIPS trainer, the person must take an annual
recertification examination. Persons who attend TIPS
training take a standardized test. If they pass the test,
the participants are issued a TIPS training card that is
effective for three years. The name of the TIPS trainer
appears on each card issued by the TIPS program.
Nicole Gehl is the Operations Manager for the Alcoholic
Beverages Division. In 2003, Ms. Gehl was responsible for
obtaining a grant from the Governor’s Traffic Safety Bureau
to allow the Division and the Iowa City Police Department
to plan and offer “value-added” TIPS training as a pilot
project to all on-premises liquor licensees in Iowa City.
The “value-added” portion of the TIPS training was law
enforcement information unique to Iowa City, such as
information on local ordinances and the procedures used in
Iowa City for alcohol compliance checks.
The Division sponsored TIPS training was four hours long
and was co-taught by Division employees and Iowa City
police officers, all of whom were certified TIPS trainers.
The Division sponsored training was offered free of charge
to all on-premises licensees in Iowa City. Ms. Gehl
personally attended the two day workshop for certification
as a TIPS trainer and conducted at least some of the
Division’s TIPS training sessions with the Iowa City police
department. (Testimony of Nicole Gehl; State Exhibits 7,
8)
3. The Division sponsored TIPS training program was
offered in Iowa City in 2003 and 2005 as a pilot project.
As part of the pilot project, the Division offered a
limited affirmative defense to licensees if the employee
completed the Division sponsored TIPS training but
subsequently sold alcohol to an underage person. The
Division distributed brochures promoting the training and
the affirmative defense to all eligible on-premises
licensees. The 2003 brochure provided the following
description of the affirmative defense:
TIPS training offered by the Iowa Alcoholic
Beverages Division through the pilot project may
be used by a licensee for a limited period as an
affirmative defense against civil penalties for

DIA No. 08DOCBL003
Page 4
alcohol sales to minors. In order for a licensee
to use the defense, the employee cited must have
been certified through the program prior to the
offense. The affirmative defense may be used
once for violations occurring after the training
takes place and may not be applied to pending
violations. Employees cited for alcohol sales to
minors may not use training as an affirmative
defense and will be subject to the same criminal
penalties as those not certified.
The 2005 brochure is nearly identical to the 2003 brochure
with respect to the affirmative defense except that it
specified that a licensee may use the affirmative defense
for a two-year period. (Testimony of Nicole Gehl; State
Exhibits 7; 8)
4. Besides the Division, there were also other groups
sponsoring TIPS training in Iowa City in 2003 and 2005.
These included employers offering in-house training
programs and beer wholesalers. While these training
programs were part of the national TIPS training program,
they did not have the value-added segment offered by the
Iowa City police department. Some of these training
programs were shorter and less thorough than the Division’s
four hour program. The Division has never granted the
affirmative defense to a licensee if the employee attended
a TIPS training program that was not sponsored by the
Division. (Testimony of Nicole Gehl)
5. On May 23, 2005, Jodie Neuzil, then an employee of the
Moose Lodge in Iowa City, completed an in-house TIPS
training program sponsored by her employer and was issued a
TIPS training certification card. Ms. Neuzil’s
certification card indicates that Christine Garling was her
TIPS trainer. Christine Garling is not an employee of the
Alcoholic Beverages Division and is not an Iowa City Police
Officer. Sometime later, Tammy Bowman hired Jodie Neuzil
to work as a server at Fitzpatrick’s. When Ms. Bowman
hired Jodie Neuzil she specifically asked her if she was
TIPS trained. Jodie Neuzil told Ms. Bowman that she had
been trained through her prior employer, and she showed Ms.
Bowman her TIPS training card. (Testimony of Tammy Bowman;
Licensee Exhibit A)
6. In August 2005, Tammy Bowman attended the TIPS
training conducted by Officer Mebus at the Sheraton Iowa

DIA No. 08DOCBL003
Page 5
City Hotel and received a TIPS training card similar to the
one issued to Jodie Neuzil. Officer Mebus told Ms. Bowman
that her TIPS training would be like a “get out of jail
free card.” Ms. Bowman assumed that Jodie Neuzil’s TIPS
training was the same as hers and that the same affirmative
defense would apply if Ms. Neuzil sold alcohol to an
underage person. (Testimony of Tammy Bowman; Nicole Gehl;
Licensee Exhibit A)
7. On October 27, 2006, employee Cole Eugene Bultman sold
an alcoholic beverage to an underage person on the premises
of Fitzpatrick’s and was later convicted under Iowa Code
section 123.49(2)(h). On February 1, 2007, the Division
imposed a $500 civil penalty on Bowman Ventures, Inc.,
d/b/a Fitzpatrick’s for a first violation of Iowa Code
section 123.49(2)(h) in a period of two years. (State
Exhibit 4)
8. On February 1 and 2, 2007, the Iowa City Police
Department conducted 36 alcohol compliance checks using
four teams of police officers and cooperating underage
persons. Prior to the compliance checks, the underage
persons were required to empty their pockets in the
officer’s presence to ensure that they carried only their
valid Iowa driver’s licenses and money issued by the police
department for making alcohol purchases. The underage
persons were instructed to answer truthfully if asked their
age and to provide their valid driver’s license if asked
for identification.
Several undercover officers and an underage male and female
entered Fitzpatrick’s shortly after midnight on February 2,
2007. The 20 year old female, SN, approached the bar and
ordered a Bud Light beer from bartender Jodie Neuzil.
Jodie Neuzil got the beer and then asked to see SN’s
identification. SN produced her driver’s license, which
had her birth date of April 15, 1986. SN’s driver’s
license was printed vertically instead of horizontally,
which indicates that SN was under the legal age when the
driver’s license was last issued. In addition, a red band
appeared above SN’s photograph with the words “Under 21
until 4-15-07.” Jodie Neuzil looked at the driver’s
license and then sold the beer to SN. One of the
undercover officers, Zach Diersen, was close enough to
observe the transaction but could not hear any conversation
between Jodie Neuzil and SN. After SN left the premises,
the officers issued Jodie Neuzil a citation for selling

DIA No. 08DOCBL003
Page 6
alcohol to an underage person, in violation of Iowa Code
section 123.49(2)(h). (Testimony of Zach Diersen; SN;
State Exhibits 1-3, 8)
9. Following a trial, Jodie Neuzil was found not guilty
of selling an alcoholic beverage to an underage person on
February 2, 2007. The criminal citation against her was
dismissed. (Testimony of Zach Diersen) On February 1,
2008, the Iowa Department of Public Safety filed a Hearing
Complaint seeking administrative sanctions against the
licensee for a second violation of Iowa Code section
123.49(2)(h) within a period of two years, based on Ms.
1
Neuzil’s sale to SN on February 2, 2007. Tammy Bowman
contacted the Division to ask for the affirmative defense
since Jodie Neuzil had completed TIPS training prior to the
sale. However, a Division employee informed Ms. Bowman
that Jodie Neuzil’s TIPS Training did not qualify for the
affirmative defense because it was not sponsored by the
Division. (Hearing Complaint; Testimony of Tammy Bowman)
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
I. Applicable Statutes and Rules
Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h)(2007) provides:
2. A person or club holding a liquor control
license or retail wine or beer permit under this
chapter, and the person's or club's agents or
employees, shall not do any of the following:
...
h. Sell, give, or otherwise supply any
alcoholic beverage, wine or beer to any person,
knowing or failing to exercise reasonable care to
ascertain whether the person is under legal age,
or permit any person, knowing or failing to
exercise reasonable care to ascertain whether the
person is under legal age, to consume any
alcoholic beverage, wine, or beer.
The Iowa Code defines "legal age" as twenty-one years of
age or more. Iowa Code section 123.3(19)(2007).
A violation of the Act or the rules of the division by any
employee, agent or servant of a licensee or permittee shall

shall subject the license or permit of said licensee or

section 123.39(1)(c).

II. Sale To Underage Person On February 2, 2007
The preponderance of the evidence established that Jodie
Neuzil, an employee of Bowman Ventures, Inc., d/b/a
Fitzpatrick’s, sold an alcoholic beverage to SN, an
underage person, on February 2, 2007. The preponderance of
the evidence further established that Jodie Neuzil either
knew or else she failed to exercise reasonable care to

DIA No. 08DOCBL003
Page 8
ascertain that SN was under the legal age. The sale
occurred under controlled circumstances with officer
witnesses. SN had an appearance and demeanor consistent
with her age, as established by the photograph taken on the
day of the compliance operation and by her appearance at
the hearing. She had been searched to ensure that she
carried only her valid driver’s license and had been
instructed to answer truthfully if asked her age. The
licensee’s employee clearly recognized that SN could be
under age and requested her identification. SN’s driver’s
license was printed vertically, which indicates that she
was under 21 when the license was issued. In addition, the
driver’s license clearly stated that SN was under 21 until
April 15, 2007. Jodie Neuzil examined the driver’s license
after SN produced it. Either Ms. Neuzil disregarded the
information on the license indicating that SN was under 21
or else she failed to examine the driver’s license
carefully enough to recognize that SN was under 21. Both
alternatives establish a violation of Iowa Code section
123.49(2)(h) because the “reasonable care” standard
requires a server to carefully examine the driver’s license
to accurately determine the customer’s age.
This was the licensee’s second violation of Iowa Code
section 123.49(2)(h) in a period of two years because the
licensee’s first violation was based on a prohibited sale
that occurred on October 27, 2006. The Iowa legislature,
through Iowa Code section 123.50(3)(b), has provided a
mandatory $1500 civil penalty and a 30 day license
suspension for a second violation of Iowa Code section
123.49(2)(h). The legislature has not provided any
exceptions to this statute nor has the Division promulgated
any rules establishing either an exception or an
affirmative defense to the statutory sanction. Based on
the applicable statutes and rules, the sanctions for a
second violation must be applied in this case.
III. Applicability of the Affirmative Defense
Since Jodie Neuzil had a current TIPS Training card when
she made the sale to SN on February 2, 2007, Tammy Bowman
believed that the licensee was entitled to assert an
affirmative defense or “get out of jail free card” for this
violation. The Division asserts that the pilot project’s
affirmative defense was only available if the offending
employee timely attended the TIPS Training sponsored by the
Alcoholic Beverages Division in conjunction with the Iowa

DIA No. 08DOCBL003
Page 9
City police department. The Division has never previously
extended the affirmative defense when the offending
employee did not complete the Division sponsored TIPS
training.
The affirmative defense offered by the Division in
conjunction with its pilot TIPS Training program was
communicated to licensees, at least in part, through
promotional brochures and at the TIPS training sessions in
2003 and 2005. The 2003 and 2005 program brochures
TIPS training
included in this record both state that “
offered by the Alcoholic Beverages Division
may be used by
a licensee...as an affirmative defense...” (emphasis
supplied). Ms. Bowman concedes that Jodie Neuzil’s TIPS
training was provided by Ms. Neuzil’s former employer and
not by the Division.
Tammy Bowman essentially argues that she was misled by the
Division’s offer to licensees of a limited affirmative
defense for violations of Iowa Code section 123.49(2)(h).
There is no entitlement to an affirmative defense under the
applicable statutes and rules; the only possible basis for
the affirmative defense was through the Division’s pilot
project. While Ms. Bowman may have misunderstood the
preconditions for claiming an affirmative defense, the
Division’s brochures only stated that the “TIPS training
offered by the Iowa Alcoholic Beverages Division” may be
used by the licensee for the affirmative defense. The
Division’s denial of an affirmative defense in this case is
consistent with its statements in these brochures. There
is no legal basis to require the Division to recognize an
affirmative defense in this case.
